summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to understand how using an imperfect volatility proxy, rather than the true latent conditional variance, can distort standard tests for comparing competing volatility forecasts, motivating both an analysis of which common loss functions are affected and a search for loss functions whose forecast rankings remain robust to proxy noise.

A researcher wants the formal definition of a robust loss function as one whose ranking of two competing volatility forecasts is unchanged whether evaluated against the true conditional variance or a conditionally unbiased proxy, together with the Diebold-Mariano-West testing framework and prior results identifying which regression-based ranking criteria already satisfy this robustness property.
summaries.answer_type: definition plus review of prior robustness results

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants a loss function taxonomy covering the nine most commonly used measures of volatility forecast accuracy, including squared-error, absolute-error, logarithmic, and proportional variants, laid out as the basis for later analytically characterising which of them produce distorted forecast rankings when the volatility proxy is noisy.

summaries.field: applied financial econometrics / volatility forecast evaluation
summaries.information_need: A researcher wants the size of the forecast distortion that arises when a squared-return volatility proxy is combined with loss functions other than MSE or QLIKE, derived analytically under Gaussian and Student's t return distributions, together with a demonstration of how conditional excess kurtosis further widens the gap between the optimal and true conditional variance forecast.

summaries.field: applied financial econometrics / volatility forecast evaluation
summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know how the forecast distortion caused by noisy loss functions shrinks when a realised volatility proxy sampled at increasing intraday frequency, or the intra-daily range, replaces the daily squared return, together with the analytical rate at which this distortion vanishes as the sampling frequency grows large.

A researcher wants the necessary and sufficient loss function functional form that guarantees a robust ranking of volatility forecasts under proxy noise, expressed as a linear-exponential combination of separate functions of the forecast and the proxy, together with the formal proof establishing this characterisation via the equivalence of robustness and optimality of the true conditional variance.

A researcher wants to know why the QLIKE loss function is the unique robust loss function depending only on the standardised forecast error, contrasted with the MSE loss function as the unique robust loss function depending only on the raw forecast error, together with the formal proof of both uniqueness results.
summaries.answer_type: uniqueness proof for two loss functions

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know how loss function homogeneity guarantees that the ranking of two imperfect volatility forecasts stays invariant to a rescaling of the data, such as a change in the units of returns, together with a counterexample showing that a robust but non-homogeneous loss function can reverse the ranking of two forecasts after rescaling.

A researcher wants the parametric loss function family, indexed by a single homogeneity parameter, that spans the entire class of robust and homogeneous loss functions and nests both MSE and QLIKE as special cases, together with the differential equation argument used to derive its closed-form expression.

summaries.field: applied financial econometrics / empirical volatility forecasting
summaries.information_need: An analyst wants an empirical forecast comparison between a rolling-window volatility model and a RiskMetrics volatility model for a liquid equity return series, evaluated across several loss functions and volatility proxies of varying sampling frequency, to see whether the ranking of the two forecasting methods changes depending on the chosen loss function.
